articles.title: Entenda a formação de geleira que teve colapso no Nepal | G1
articles.standfirst: Bloco de gelo de 600 metros se desprendeu de geleira e provocou rompimento de lago; nível de rio chegou a subir 9 metros em meia hora.
articles.summary: Bloco de gelo de 600 metros se desprendeu de geleira e provocou rompimento de lago; nível de rio chegou a subir 9 metros em meia hora.
articles.body:
O colapso de uma geleira provocou as enchentes catastróficas no Nepal , de acordo com o USGS (Serviço Geológico dos Estados Unidos). O desastre já soma mais de 300 mortes e centenas de desaparecidos no que é uma das piores tragédias do país em mais de dez anos.

A região tem uma geografia montanhosa e abriga as maiores montanhas do mundo. Entre elas está o Langtang Lirung, com 7.245 metros – onde houve o colapso.

De acordo com especialistas, a geleira que caiu tinha cerca de 600 metros de largura. O impacto de sua queda foi tamanho que o USGS chegou a sinalizar na quarta-feira (26) que a região tinha passado por um terremoto de escala 5,2. Na verdade, depois se descobriu que a que o abalo aconteceu por causa da queda do gelo e o deslizamento de rochas na encosta da montanha.

Em regiões de altitude muito elevada, a precipitação não cai em forma líquida. Por causa das baixas temperaturas, a chuva se transforma em gelo antes de atingir o solo.

Para se ter uma ideia, no monte Everest, que fica na região, em algumas épocas do ano a temperatura pode chegar a -50°C.

Esse acúmulo se repete ano após ano, ao longo de milhares a milhões de anos, formando as geleiras.

Entenda a formação de geleiras e o rompimento que provocou enchente repentina no Nepal — Foto: Arte/g1

Não há ainda como saber o que causou esse desprendimento de uma massa de gelo tão grande. O que os especialistas explicam é que ainda que sejam massas de água em estado sólido, as geleiras não são estáticas.

“Elas se movimentam naturalmente, seja pela queda de blocos de gelo mais antigo ou deslizamento de camadas de neve mais recente. É um ambiente bastante instável”, explica o geólogo Julio Lana, do Serviço Geológico do Brasil (SGB).

Em artigo no The Conversation, Levan Tielidze - pesquisador em geomorfologia glacial na Universidade Monash - lembra que o terreno na região, formado pelo permafrost, pode ter se desestabilizado .

Pesquisas recentes mostram que o calor causado pela mudança do clima vem impactando as geleiras no mundo. E o aquecimento global pode estar fazendo com que o permafrost — solo, sedimento ou rocha que permanece congelado por longos períodos — descongele e se degrade.

O permafrost ajuda a manter algumas encostas de montanhas unidas. Quando ele perde estabilidade, esses ambientes de alta montanha podem ficar mais instáveis.

No entanto, ainda é cedo para dizer que o que houve no Nepal tem relação com a mudança do clima.

E o que houve depois que o gelo se desprendeu?

Esse ponto ainda não está totalmente esclarecido. A hipótese mais provável, segundo o especialista, é a de que o bloco de gelo tenha caído dentro de um lago glacial — reservatórios de água formados ao longo do tempo pelo derretimento parcial das próprias geleiras, comuns nas encostas do Himalaia.

Essas regiões guardam dezenas de lagos desse tipo, alguns com milhares de litros de água acumulada.

Ao cair dentro do lago, o bloco expulsou parte da água represada ali e rompeu as barreiras naturais que a continham — formadas por rochas soltas e sedimentos, e não por rocha maciça. O fenômeno tem nome técnico: GLOF, sigla em inglês para rompimento de lago glacial.

Para se ter uma ideia de como isso funciona: é como jogar uma pedra em um copo com água que transborda quase que instantaneamente.

“Essa força da água é tanta que empurra esses blocos de rocha que represam a água desses lagos. Eles então vazam e percorrem a região, conectando a outros desses lagos, acumulando um volume alto de água. Isso explica um pouco o volume da avalanche que vimos”, explica o geólogo Julio Lana, do Serviço Geológico do Brasil (SGB).

Lago glacial em geleira no Alasca — Foto: Becky Bohrer/AP Photo

O resultado desse acúmulo apareceu na velocidade da cheia: o nível do rio Trishuli subiu até 9 metros em apenas 30 minutos. Um evento que começou a quilômetros de distância, no alto da cordilheira, chegou às áreas habitadas em questão de minutos — sem tempo hábil de reação para quem estava no caminho.

E ainda se soma ao contexto da região: o Nepal passa pela época de monções — período do ano em que a chuva é mais intensa.

Esse tipo de evento não é incomum no Himalaia. Desde 1900, a região já registrou mais de 100 rompimentos de lagos glaciais, resultando em cerca de 7 mil mortes ao longo desse período, segundo estudo publicado em 2022 na revista científica Science of the Total Environment.

O levantamento também mostra que, ao contrário do que se poderia supor, lagos pequenos — historicamente ignorados em avaliações de risco — têm protagonizado uma parcela crescente desses rompimentos desde a década de 1980.

articles.title: Glacier sheared off, plunged 1.2km before ‘liquid concrete’ flood swamped Nepal
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nearly two-thirds of a high-altitude glacier near the Nepal-Tibet border sheared away and plunged about 1.2km into the Lhende Khola river catchment We.
articles.body: Nearly two-thirds of a high-altitude glacier near the Nepal-Tibet border sheared away and plunged about 1.2km into the Lhende Khola river catchment Wednesday. This triggered a chain reaction in which falling ice gathered rock, snow and sediment, temporarily blocked the river and then released a debris-laden torrent into the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor, satellite analysis and scientists’ assessments showed. The collapse occurred on the Nepalese side of the border.Satellite images analysed by Isro’s national remote sensing centre showed that almost two-thirds of the glacier body had detached. A Sentinel-2 image from Aug 24 showed the glacier intact, while a Landsat-9 image taken after the disaster on Aug 26 revealed a large scar identified as the “zone of glacier breakage and collapse”. The images also traced a broad ice-rock avalanche path descending towards the river.The scale of the fall was crucial to what happened next. Daniel Shugar, a geomorphologist at the University of Calgary, estimated from Planet Labs imagery that roughly 200 square metres of ice broke off at an altitude of around 5,200 metres and “collapsed about 1.2km vertically” to the valley floor. The drop “converted enormous gravitational energy into motion, allowing the mass to break apart and sweep up loose material rather than remaining a relatively coherent block of ice”.As the avalanche descended, it bulked up. Simon Cox, principal scientist at Earth Sciences New Zealand, said the collapsing glacier transformed into “a very large debris flow”, picking up rocks, sediment, trees and other material in its path.That sequence explained why the flood behaved very differently from an ordinary rise in river water. Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at University of Texas at San Antonio, described such fast-moving mud-and-water flows as “like liquid concrete” — dense enough to sweep away vehicles, structures and large boulders rather than simply flow around them. articles.title: NHS bosses warn of chaos in ADHD and autism care
articles.summary: Costs are spiralling out of control as unregulated private providers capitalise on demand, say managers.
articles.body:
Autism and ADHD care is at risk of descending into chaos, NHS bosses are warning, as costs spiral out of control and unregulated private providers capitalise on the huge demand for help.

The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, says the current system represents a "bad deal" for patients and taxpayers alike.

It points to big variations in what the NHS is being charged for assessments and care - in one case, a local health board was paying £300 to £3,000 for similar services.

The group says there has been a rapid expansion in new providers – both private firms and charities are involved - and NHS managers are struggling to ensure the quality and safety of care being provided.

The government said an independent review into services would be published soon and it would act on the findings of that, promising a “new national approach” for autism, ADHD and mental health.

Ahead of that, the NHS Alliance has been gathering information from integrated care boards, which hold the budgets for local services, about the current state of care.

A split in the spectrum? The ongoing battle to define autism

Under the right to choose policy, patients can decide to opt for care from both NHS and non-NHS autism and ADHD services.

The initiative is aimed at helping patients bypass the long waiting lists that have developed in recent years.

The NHS Alliance said the policy has led to an influx of new providers, helping to reduce some of the longest waits for adults and children, but at a cost.

It found a number of boards were reporting sharp rises in spending, describing it as "out of control".

One board saw costs rising 10-fold in a year, to £1.5m a month.

Another saw annual spend jump from £4m a year to £30m over the course of two years.

It said a particular problem was the huge variation in what was being charged by non-NHS providers.

Unlike for routine operations, like hip and knee replacements, where there is a set tariff for different treatments regardless of whether the NHS or private sector carry them out, for autism and ADHD there are only guide prices that do not have to be kept to.

Local health bosses have also reported a rapid increase in providers. One board reported working with 48 providers – four times more than in two years previously.

This expansion was causing problems with the ability of boards to check the quality and safety of the care and support being provided.

Providers who carry out assessments only do not have to be registered with the Care Quality Commission, the regulatory body for health and care.

Rebecca Gray of the NHS Alliance said managers were "caught between a rock and a hard place".

"They understand the anguish and frustration caused by long delays in the system as people wait for assessments, treatment and support.

"But in working to meeting demand they face soaring costs that are running out of control."

She said the situation was a "bad deal for patients and taxpayers" and there was a risk the whole system would fall into "chaos".

Mel Merritt, of the National Autistic Society, said it was clear the system was in crisis.

"Spending is rising on short-term solutions due to years of a lack of long-term investment in improving services."

And she added despite the sums being spent people were still facing "unacceptable" delays.

articles.title: UK weather: thunderstorms and rain forecast for bank holiday weekend
articles.summary: The weather will remain unsettled across the next few days with showers, longer spells of rain and thunderstorms all likely at times across the weekend.
articles.body:
Most of the UK is finally getting some rain, in time for the bank holiday weekend.

The weather will remain unsettled across the next few days with showers, longer spells of rain and thunderstorms all likely at times.

By Monday the focus of the wet weather is likely to be across Scotland, with sunny spells developing elsewhere.

The RAC estimates that 20 million trips by car will be made across the weekend in what could be challenging driving conditions.

Friday could see heavy downpours and more thunderstorms

Showers and longer spells of rain will continue to affect the UK on Friday, with heavy downpours and thunderstorms possible, especially across western Scotland, Wales and north-west England.

Some of this wet weather could spread east later, with thunderstorms possible across north-east England and eastern Scotland.

After the recent warm and humid conditions, temperatures by Friday will feel fresher.

Expect around 20–23C (68 -73F) in England and Wales, and 16–20C (61-68F) in Scotland and Northern Ireland.

These temperatures are around average for late August.

Continuing risk of thunderstorms with more rain for Saturday, Sunday and Monday

Saturday will remain unsettled, with sunny spells mixed with heavy showers and possible thunderstorms, particularly across England and Wales.

Fresh westerly winds will make it feel blustery, with highs of 18-22C (64-72F) in England and Wales and 16-19C (61-66F) further north.

Sunday and Bank Holiday Monday - for England and Wales - will stay changeable, with further heavy showers, longer spells of rain and a risk of thunderstorms once again.

Monday is likely to be wettest across Scotland, while England and Wales can expect a mix of sunshine and showers before further rain moves in from the west.

Stronger winds are also possible across southern parts of the UK, with temperatures generally ranging from 16C to 23C (61-73F).

Why are there no thunderstorms showing on my app?

No September heatwave currently in sight

Overall, the late August bank holiday weekend looks set to be cooler, windier and wetter than the hot and dry conditions we've experienced for much of this record-breaking summer.

There will still be some pleasant sunny spells between showers, with temperatures potentially reaching the low 20s in the south-east.

However, with low pressure remaining close to the UK, there is currently little sign of a return to prolonged hot and settled weather.

The outlook for early September suggests further changeable conditions, with a mixture of sunshine and showers and temperatures generally close to or slightly below average.

Whatever your plans for the weekend, you can keep up to date with the forecast by checking the BBC Weather website and app .

articles.title: Chad accuses Sudan of air strike near shared border that killed 12
articles.summary: An air strike on a fuel market near Chad’s border with Sudan killed 12 and injured seven, according to officials.
articles.body:
An air strike near Chad’s border with Sudan has killed at least 12 people, with Chad accusing the Sudanese army of launching it.

Addressing Thursday’s strike, a Chadian security source said it “targeted a fuel market where the RSF [Rapid Support Forces] refuel. The strike killed 12 people and wounded seven”, AFP news agency reported about the attack on the paramilitary group.

Chad’s accusation comes against the backdrop of a civil war between Sudan’s army and the RSF which has lasted over three years and displaced millions of people.

Previously, Chad said that Sudan was responsible for an air strike that hit a military convoy in its territory last week. Chad’s army said the strikes took place more than 100km (62 miles) inside its territory in the eastern Ennedi region, and that there were no Chadian casualties.

In response to threats posed by drones, Chad had raised its alert level in the area to its highest point, according to a security source. The country deployed about 100 armoured vehicles and signal-jamming trucks near eastern Tine, close to the Sudanese border, a local source told Reuters news agency.

On Thursday, Sudan said it was surprised by the allegations against its army “before any professional and independent investigation into the circumstances of the incident”.

Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said its forces “are carrying out their constitutional duty to protect Sudan’s sovereignty, security and safety and to face any threats it faces, while respecting the sovereignty of its neighbours and without targeting their territory”.

The US embassy in Khartoum also accused the Sudanese army of launching the recent strikes on Chad, condemning them on Thursday.

The Sudanese army has previously accused Chad of being aligned with the RSF. Meanwhile, nearly one million displaced Sudanese people have fled to Chad, where they have been facing a water crisis .

articles.title: Maine meteorologist suffers giggle attack on live TV after prank backfires spectacularly
articles.summary: Patrick Osborn struggled to finish his WABI weather report after a prank involving Charlie Brown audio sent him into a fit of laughter.
articles.body: A local meteorologist is experiencing viral fame after he was caught on live television suddenly breaking into an uncontrollable fit of giggles that grew increasingly hysterical as he struggled to keep his composure. Patrick Osborn, who was delivering a regularly scheduled weather report on Maine news station WABI, left viewers completely stunned Sunday morning as he repeatedly tried, and failed, to hold back his laughter. In the video, Osborn was seen gasping for breath as he blurted out temperatures between chuckles, repeatedly apologizing before the laughter finally rendered his speech completely incomprehensible. The laughing fit stretched on for about a minute, with Osborn stepping off camera before returning and eventually tossing back to a colleague. SPORTS COMMENTATOR MICHAEL HOLLEY IS 'FINE' AFTER FAINTING DURING LIVE BROADCAST IN TERRIFYING SCENE Recalling the moment with WABI co-anchor Brian Sullivan, Osborn said, "I got a fit of laughter that I was not able to control on air, unfortunately. A lot of times, something funny happens, and I’m able to contain myself, but this one, it was just a little too overwhelming." He revealed that the laughter was triggered by a prank he had attempted to play on fellow anchor Josh Gabbard, only for the joke to backfire on him. During a commercial break, Osborn said he played a short Charlie Brown video for its sound effects but failed to realize the clip was actually an hour-long compilation that periodically replayed the sound every few minutes. DAD JOKES MAY BE GOOD FOR YOUR BRAIN IN ONE SURPRISING WAY, EXPERTS SAY He said the audio then unexpectedly played again while he was starting his weather segment, almost instantly sending him into hysterical laughter. "It’s the Charlie Brown phone call noise. It’s one where his mom or teacher calls him, and it’s the ‘Wa, wa, wa,’" Osborn told his station. "Something as silly and light-hearted as a Charlie Brown sound made me completely lose my composure." "I was just trying to keep it together but I couldn't. Like, when you're not supposed to laugh, you're in an environment when you can't laugh, and you're trying to hold it back, that just makes it 10 times worse," he said. Osborn added: "I tried to get through it," but "Josh had to leave the studio." articles.title: Federal US judge faces complaint over staunch pro-Israel advocacy
articles.summary: A lawyer has accused Judge Roy Altman, who calls the keffiyeh a ‘terror scarf’, of anti-Palestinian bias in his remarks.
articles.body:
A federal judge in the United States is facing a formal complaint over anti-Palestinian comments and alleged association with Islamophobic groups, in a case that highlights growing concern about possible pro-Israel bias in the judicial system .

Florida lawyer Katherine Giannamore filed the judicial complaint against District Judge Roy Altman earlier this month, accusing him of eroding “public confidence in the integrity, impartiality, and independence of the federal judiciary”.

The complaint, filed with the Eleventh Circuit Court, also says Altman used judicial resources to promote Israel, including by making media appearances from his chambers in Miami.

“Since at least April 2026, Judge Altman has consistently engaged in this conduct during business hours, broadcasting himself live from chambers and has utilized law clerks during public talks during business hours,” the complaint reads.

“These activities have been persistent, almost daily and spanned several months.”

The complaint points to several examples of what it considers to be worrying behaviour.

In April, for instance, Judge Altman appeared on a podcast with the Middle East Forum, a right-wing group whose stated mission is to combat “the infrastructure of lawful Islamism”. During the interview, he called the keffiyeh , a symbol of Palestinian identity, a “terrorism scarf”.

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Giannamore pointed to such remarks as a reason for concern.

“This kind of blatant use of the judicial office for your own political aspirations or your beliefs, it’s bad for the judiciary. It’s bad for public opinion as far as the legitimacy of the judiciary,” Giannamore said.

She acknowledged that the complaint is unlikely to lead to a reprimand against Altman, but she said it was important to raise the issue.

Federal judges are appointed for life. Judicial misconduct complaints go to the chief judge of a court of appeals, who can either dismiss them or appoint a special committee to investigate the claims.

In rare cases, the complaints can lead to sanctions, including the decision to suspend case assignments to a given judge or a request for voluntary resignation.

Giannamore believes complaints like hers can help spark a discussion about acceptable behaviour within the judicial system, particularly for lifelong office-holders.

“It’s important to bring awareness to that, and maybe give them a moment to take a step back and say, ‘Is this worth it? Is this something that we accept? And would we accept it if it was other issues that a judge was using the office to speak on?'” Giannamore said.

Altman, a staunch supporter of Israel who was appointed by President Donald Trump in 2019, is currently promoting a self-published book defending the US ally.

During his remarks with the Middle East Forum in April, he explained that he had been touring college campuses and churches to dismiss accusations of rights abuses against Israel, which has been carrying out a genocidal war on Gaza.

The judge uses “Jews” and “Israel” interchangeably throughout his talks.

“I say on college campuses, ‘You think you’re counterculture? You think you’re cool and unique because you wear the terrorism scarf, the keffiyeh, and you chant against the Jews? Get in line, get a ticket. You’re the most mainstream, boring thing history has ever seen,'” Altman said.

That was one of several incidents in which the judge demonised the symbol of Palestinian nationalism.

“At Yale Law School, for example, in three years, I graduated in 2007, I never once saw a single person wearing a keffiyeh,” he said on a recent podcast.

“And so that tells you that, at one of the most liberal law schools on the planet, not one student thought it was appropriate to wear a scarf that is a symbol of terrorism and the deaths — the violent deaths of thousands and thousands of innocent Jews.”

Altman is also a prolific social media user, and most of his posts are about Israel. He has also made frequent appearances on podcasts and in YouTube clips.

In one interview, he declared that “there is no distinction” between anti-Semitism and anti-Zionism .

The judge’s pro-Israel advocacy at times drifts into comments that could be seen as hostile towards Arabs and Muslims.

“The real geo-strategic conflict here isn’t seven million Jews against six million Palestinians,” he said in June.

“It’s seven million Jews surrounded by two billion Muslims — hundreds of millions of whom have been raised to believe that divine providence requires them to devote their lives to the destruction of that teeny, tiny Jewish state.”

The judge did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by the time of publication.

It is highly unusual for a judge to be so outspoken about a divisive political issue.

Altman’s advocacy comes at a time when the federal judiciary is assessing several cases relating to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including Trump’s push to deport student activists who protested against the war on Gaza.

Altman often promotes a travel programme by the World Jewish Congress to take fellow judges on trips to Israel — visits akin to the junkets the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) gives to members of Congress.

“One of the reasons our judges in America give for why trips to Israel are so profoundly transformative for them is that, in Israel, you can feel our joint Judeo-Christian heritage, our history, our home,” he wrote in a social media post earlier this month.

According to Giannamore’s complaint, Altman said in a speech at Florida International University that he has taken 10 percent of the federal judiciary on such trips.

Such a large number of judges “coming away from foreign state-sponsored trips, where they meet with foreign political officials, is truly frightening”, the complaint said. It pointed out that some of those judges may rule on cases related to Israel.

Giannamore suggested that possible bias acquired from the “propaganda” visits to Israel may extend beyond issues related to the conflict, but to cases involving Palestinians , Arabs and Muslims more broadly.

“It goes into biases that they at least can be perceived to hold versus Palestinians, Arabs, Muslims, peace advocates,” she said.

“So if you’re taking 10 percent of the judiciary right now and they’re spread all across the country, that’s a huge number, and I think that ultimately undermines public confidence in one of our branches of government. So, it’s really bad for everyone.”

articles.title: Fired Stars and Stripes staffers sue Pentagon, allege retaliation and First Amendment violation
articles.summary: Fired Stars and Stripes staffers allege the Pentagon retaliated against them for First Amendment-protected speech and USS Abraham Lincoln reporting.
articles.body: The three Stars and Stripes staffers who were fired last week over alleged insubordination have filed a lawsuit against the Pentagon over their terminations, alleging they are facing "imminent retaliation and termination in violation of their First Amendment and statutory rights." "Defendants are attempting to fire Plaintiffs for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations, its need to reach all servicepersons, and in retaliation for their publication of a news report on deteriorating conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln during its extended tour of duty in the Mid-East," the lawsuit filed Thursday stated. "This action seeks to prevent the blatant violation of the First Amendment rights of these journalists and challenges the U.S. Department of Defense’s extraordinary censorship efforts in violation of both the First Amendment and DoD regulations and policies." The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., was brought by ousted Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, longtime publisher Max Lederer and Middle East reporter Lara Korte. PENTAGON FIRES LONGTIME PUBLISHER, EDITOR, REPORTER FROM MILITARY NEWSPAPER STARS AND STRIPES The firings stem from Slavin and Korte's unauthorized participation in a "CBS Sunday Morning" segment that aired last month about the Pentagon's efforts to overhaul the paper and Lederer's refusal to fire them at the direction of Pentagon leadership. According to the lawsuit, the trio allege Pentagon leadership "understood these interview statements expressed personal opinions, and therefore took no immediate action, despite their displeasure" and that it wasn't until Stars and Stripes published its report on the alleged strife aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln that the Pentagon's stance had shifted. The lawsuit notes that Pentagon leadership demanded Lederer to fire Slavin and Korte just one day after the report was published. PENTAGON OFFICIALS MULLING THE FIRING OF MILITARY NEWSPAPER STARS AND STRIPES PUBLISHER Listed as the defendants in the lawsuit are The Pentagon, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell and his principal deputy assistant Andrew Brey. "Our goal is to protect the rights of service members and their families to a free and independent press," Slavin, Lederer and Korte said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Stars and Stripes has served them for generations, and that independence is essential to keeping military communities fully and accurately informed." "This lawsuit is about safeguarding that mission and ensuring our civilian and military journalists can do their jobs without retaliation," they added. PENTAGON VOWS TO REFORM MILITARY NEWSPAPER STARS AND STRIPES, REMOVE 'WOKE DISTRACTIONS' A Pentagon spokesman declined to comment. The Pentagon kicked off 2026 by announcing its overhaul of the long-running newspaper. "The Department of War is returning Stars & Stripes to its original mission: reporting for our warfighters," Parnell posted on X in January. "We are bringing Stars & Stripes into the 21st century. We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members. "Stars & Stripes will be custom tailored to our warfighters. It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability, and ALL THINGS MILITARY," the statement continued. "No more repurposed DC gossip columns; no more Associated Press reprints. Stars & Stripes has a proud legacy of reporting news that’s important to our service members. The Department of War is committed to ensuring the outlet continues to reflect that proud legacy." The Pentagon previously fired the Stars and Stripes ombudsman in April after being an outspoken critic of the Trump administration's oversight of the paper. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: California authorities identify final unknown victim of ‘Happy Face Killer’ Keith Jesperson after 34 years
articles.summary: DNA testing confirmed Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter as the 'Happy Face Killer's' final unidentified victim, found along a California highway in 1992.
articles.body: The final unidentified victim of notorious serial killer Keith Hunter Jesperson, known as the "Happy Face Killer," has been identified more than three decades after her body was discovered along a California highway, authorities announced Thursday. The Riverside County District Attorney's Office identified the woman, long known to investigators only as "Claudia," as Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter of Texas, after DNA testing confirmed a connection to a member of her maternal family. McWhorter's body was discovered Aug. 30, 1992, along Highway 95 about seven miles north of Blythe, California. Jesperson, a long-haul truck driver who confessed to killing eight women across multiple states, later admitted killing her. Jesperson told investigators he knew the woman as "Claudia," but authorities were unable to determine whether that was her real name. INVESTIGATORS FIND RELATIVES OF ‘HAPPY FACE’ SERIAL KILLER’S LAST UNKNOWN VICTIM IN MISSION TO IDENTIFY HER The identification comes after Riverside County investigators publicly renewed their effort to identify McWhorter in 2024, when genetic genealogy had connected the unknown victim to relatives on her father's side but had not produced the maternal connection needed to confirm her identity. Fox News Digital reported at the time that DNA testing had identified Summer Gonzales as the victim's paternal half-sister. Gonzales said she wanted to learn her sister's real name and eventually lay her to rest with family. An investigative lead ultimately brought the cold case team to one of McWhorter's direct maternal relatives, according to the district attorney's office. Investigators then identified a possible genetic connection to another member of the maternal family. A DNA sample confirmed that connection earlier this week, allowing investigators to positively identify McWhorter nearly 34 years after her body was found, authorities said. REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY McWhorter's sisters, who grew up with her, had spent decades without knowing what happened to her after she disappeared from Texas in the 1990s, according to prosecutors. "I want to thank the public for the role you play in our investigations," Billy Hester, supervising investigator of the Cold Case Unit, said in a news release. "When people take the time to share information, submit a tip or simply pay attention to what is happening in their community, it can make a real difference. You may not know where a piece of information will lead, but our investigators will follow it. Most importantly, I hope this will finally bring closure to Lydia’s family." The district attorney's Division of Victim Services is working with McWhorter's family as they decide how to honor her and lay her to rest. 'HAPPY FACE' KILLER WARNS FELLOW SERIAL KILLER REX HEUERMANN COULD BE 'TOSSED TO THE WOLVES' IN PRISON Jesperson was arrested in 1995, and eventually confessed to killing eight women between 1990 and 1995 in California, Washington state, Oregon, Florida, Nebraska and Wyoming. He became known as the "Happy Face Killer" after sending letters about his crimes to the media that he signed with a smiley face. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He pleaded guilty to McWhorter's murder in Riverside County on Jan. 8, 2010, and was sentenced to 25 years to life in prison. He is serving multiple life sentences in Oregon. With McWhorter's identification, Riverside County's cold case team has now closed the final unidentified-victim case tied to the murders for which Jesperson was convicted.

articles.title: Australia’s ancient red desert rocks may be hiding a natural hydrogen secret; scientists find magnetite produces 5 times more hydrogen than solid rock
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Beneath Western Australia’s iron-rich landscapes, ordinary looking rocks may have a unique ability to produce hydrogen. A new study published in the ‘.
articles.body: Beneath Western Australia’s iron-rich landscapes, ordinary looking rocks may have a unique ability to produce hydrogen. A new study published in the ‘International Journal of Hydrogen Energy’ has found that magnetite, an iron oxide found in many ancient rocks, can generate natural hydrogen when it reacts with water under hot, high-pressure conditions. The research focuses on a question that ‘does the physical shape of the rock affect how much hydrogen it can produce.’ The answer appears to be yes. In controlled experiments, finely powdered magnetite produced about 5 times more hydrogen than intact slabs of the same material. The finding does not prove that a huge underground fuel supply is ready to be extracted, but it shows why the structure, surface area and pathways through hydrogen-bearing rocks could be crucial to understanding this energy source.Production of hydrogen from Australia’s Red desert magnetiteThe study examines how magnetite behaves when exposed to hot water. Magnetite is an iron-rich mineral that occurs in a range of geological formations. The researchers were interested in natural hydrogen, which is produced through geological processes rather than manufactured using industrial methods. Their work examined whether magnetite could generate hydrogen under conditions involving hot water deep underground. The important discovery was not simply that magnetite can produce hydrogen. Earlier research had already indicated that possibility. Instead, this study investigated how the physical form of the mineral affects the amount of hydrogen produced. That distinction is important because rocks underground are not usually present as loose powder. They occur as solid formations, often with limited spaces through which water can move.How the researchers tested natural magnetiteTo investigate the effect of rock geometry, the researchers compared natural magnetite in two forms. A fine powder and an intact slab. Both were exposed to the same experimental conditions. The tests were conducted at 200°C, a pressure of 103.4 bar and a pH of 9, with the experiments running for 60 days. By keeping the same conditions, the researchers could focus on whether the shape and exposed surface of the magnetite changed hydrogen production. The results showed a striking difference. The powdered magnetite produced 0.052 millimoles of hydrogen per gram of rock. The intact slab produced 0.0105 millimoles per gram. In other words, the powder generated roughly 5 times as much hydrogen as the solid slab under the same conditions. The result suggests that ‘simply knowing how much magnetite exists in an underground formation may not be enough to estimate its hydrogen-generating potential.Importance of shape of the rock in hydrogen productionThe main reason appears to be the amount of ‘mineral surface’ available for the reaction. A fine powder has many small particles and a large amount of exposed surface. Water can come into contact with far more of the magnetite, creating more opportunities for the chemical reaction that produces hydrogen. An intact rock slab is different. Much of its magnetite remains inside the rock and is difficult for water to reach. The study found that the solid samples were affected by limitations on how easily fluids could move through and reach reactive areas. The researchers also found evidence that the surface of the magnetite changed during the experiment. The slab became rougher, while microscopic examination showed changes in its texture and the development of small porous features. These changes matter because they can alter the way water interacts with the mineral over time.Could this change the search for natural hydrogenThe findings could influence how scientists think about underground hydrogen resources. If hydrogen production depends strongly on surface area and the movement of water, then exploration cannot focus only on finding rocks containing large amounts of magnetite. Researchers may also need to understand fractures, pores and other features that allow water to reach reactive parts of a geological formation. This is particularly relevant to ‘magnetite-bearing banded iron formations,’ which can occur over large areas. The study specifically highlights the importance of these formations and other magnetite-rich rocks when considering natural hydrogen production and geological hydrogen storage.However, the findings should not be interpreted as proof of a massive underground hydrogen reserve ready for commercial extraction. The experiments were conducted under controlled lab conditions, and the study itself focuses on understanding the chemical and physical factors that influence hydrogen generation. Natural rock formations are much more complicated. Their permeability, fractures, mineral composition and fluid movement can vary considerably from one location to another. Instead of asking only how much magnetite is present, future investigations may need to ask how easily water can reach it. Western Australia’s rocks may have the ingredients for natural hydrogen generation, but understanding how that process works in real geological formations will be essential before its energy potential can be properly assessed. The study’s central finding is straightforward: ‘when it comes to natural hydrogen, the shape of the rock can matter almost as much as the rock itself.’Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal floods death toll rises to 469 as China warns of fresh washout threat
articles.summary: South Asia News: The death toll from the devastating flash floods along Nepal’s border with Tibet has risen to 469, Nepal Police said on Friday, as rescue teams contin.
articles.body: The death toll from the devastating flash floods along Nepal’s border with Tibet has risen to 469, Nepal Police said on Friday, as rescue teams continue searching for people missing after a torrent of water, mud and debris swept through the region earlier this week.Massive landslides and flooding struck the mountainous border area on Wednesday, causing widespread destruction across northern Nepal and parts of Tibet. Rescue and evacuation operations have continued, with military personnel and helicopters deployed to reach affected communities and search for survivors.The disaster has also raised fears of further flooding after China issued a Level-IV emergency alert over a newly formed barrier lake near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers. The rivers originate in Tibet and flow into Nepal as part of the Bhote Koshi river system.China’s Ministry of Water Resources said the lake had accumulated around two million cubic metres of water by Thursday morning. Forecasts suggested inflows could reach about three million cubic metres over the following three days amid continued rainfall, raising the risk that the lake could breach and send more water downstream.Authorities are closely monitoring the lake, rainfall and downstream areas, while identifying communities that could be at risk. The potential impact includes areas around Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border.China has also deployed satellites, drones and unmanned aerial vehicles to support rescue and assessment operations. Satellite imagery is being used to assess the affected areas, while high-definition and thermal imaging equipment is helping rescue teams identify priority search zones and locate possible survivors in vegetation and mud-covered areas.The flooding was initially thought to have been triggered by an earthquake, but the US Geological Survey said the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse". The collapse was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 event as the glacier hit the valley floor, according to USGS data.Scientists believe the collapse sent huge amounts of ice, rock and sediment into the river system, triggering catastrophic downstream flooding. Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the sequence may have involved a landslide blocking the river before the accumulated water burst through in a massive flood.The disaster sent a wall of mud and water through northern Nepal, destroying buildings, roads and vehicles. Severe flooding was reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers, while deaths were also reported on the Tibetan side of the border.Scientists are continuing to examine satellite imagery, rainfall data and evidence of possible river blockages to establish exactly how the disaster unfolded.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal floods swept ​bodies 200km downstream, 3 found in UP
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Barely seven minutes separated the seismic signal generated by Wednesday’s Himalayan collapse from the destructive surge reaching Rasuwagad.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Barely seven minutes separated the seismic signal generated by Wednesday’s Himalayan collapse from the destructive surge reaching Rasuwagadhi at the Nepal-Tibet border, but the flood’s trail stretched nearly 200km downstream. Bodies were recovered through Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Nawalparasi East, while three more, believed to have been swept out of Nepal, were found in the Gandak river in Maharajganj, Uttar Pradesh, on Thursday. Chitwan, along Nepal’s border with India, recorded 132 recoveries — the highest in any district.The initial seismic signal was recorded at 8.37am. Border-security footage showed people fleeing moments before the torrent tore through the narrow gorge, sweeping away buildings and vehicles. The seven-minute interval reflected the speed at which the disaster unfolded, but did not amount to an official evacuation window: Nepal’s flood authorities received information about the surge only after it had entered Bhote Koshi.Sauharda Joshi, hydrologist at Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, said the flood crossed into Nepal at around 8.40am and reached Syabrubesi within about 10 minutes. “If we had been informed while the flood was building up in Tibet, human casualties could have been significantly minimised,” he said.Flood Forecasting Division received information about the major surge at 9.05am and sent more than 600,000 SMS warnings to people along riverbanks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan within minutes. The flood later moved through Trishuli into the Narayani river, carrying its debris trail towards Nepal’s southern plains.The trail continued into India as Narayani becomes Gandak downstream. SSB teams recovered bodies of two women and a man in Maharajganj. SSB inspector Arun Pandey said, “Three bodies believed to have been swept into the Gandak from Nepal have so far been recovered in Indian territory.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jake Reiner says he hasn’t spoken to his brother as he opens up about grief after parents’ deaths
articles.summary: “I will never understand why this happened,” Jake Reiner told KABC-TV of Los Angeles about the murders of Rob Reiner and Michelle Singer Reiner. His brother has been charged in their deaths.
articles.body: It has been eight months since beloved Hollywood director Rob Reiner and his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, were killed and their son Nick Reiner was arrested in their deaths. But for Jake Reiner, the couple’s 35-year-old son, the nightmare feels like “eight years at the same time, and it also feels like eight minutes,” he told KABC-TV of Los Angeles in his first sit-down interview since the family tragedy. “Every moment that I wake up, I’m reminded of my reality, and you’re living through that every single day,” he said. Jake said he hasn’t spoken to his brother. Nor has he attended any of his brother’s court hearings, the station reported. “He’s in jail, so, you know, it’s like I physically lost my parents and then Nick was arrested. And it’s like now, it’s just me and Romy,” he said, referring to his 28-year-old sister. Jake opened up to KABC in the interview, which aired Thursday, about navigating grief and how it can manifest into anger. “I’ll never understand. I don’t care how it’s explained to me. I don’t care what facts come out. I will never understand why this happened,” he told the station. “It manifests into rage, into how unfair this was. How I didn’t get a say in what happened. I didn’t get to stop it from happening. I had no choice in the matter, and I just have to accept the reality of it. And to me that is just one of the most infuriating parts of all this,” he said. Rob Reiner, 78, and Michele Singer Reiner, 70, were found brutally stabbed in their home in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles on Dec. 14. Nick was arrested hours later. Jake was at Los Angeles’ Union Station for a celebration of life event for a friend when his sister called. He didn’t pick up. “She called immediately again, and I knew at that point something immediately was wrong. Romy told me our dad was dead, and then she said, ‘I can’t find Mom.’ And I immediately went into shock. I need to get out of this train station, and I need to get to my parents’ house,” he recalled. Asked whether he was surprised to learn that his brother was the main suspect, Jake took a deep breath and said, “I feel like that’s something I don’t really want to answer right now.” In April, Jake wrote about his heartbreak on Substack, saying, “We lost more than half of our family that night in the most violent way imaginable.” He affirmed that that included Nick. Nick Reiner, 32, has a long history of drug addiction and has struggled with his mental health. He co-wrote the 2016 movie “Being Charlie” with his father, who directed it, about the experiences of a young man who struggles with recovery. “I can tell you, they never stopped wanting to help him. They never stopped helping him,” Jake said of his parents’ supporting Nick. “And I think that project was a way for my dad to try and connect with him.” Asked whether it was ever a fear that something like the murders could ever happen, Jake declined to answer. Now his focus is on following in his parents’ footsteps working with the Children’s Institute, an organization that supports children and families. He’ll be at its gala in November. “It’s going to be hard. I think everything that we’ve done so far without them has been hard and weird. But I do feel responsible for making sure people know them and they remember them,” he said. Nick Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder in connection with special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and lying in wait. His case continues in court. Earlier this summer, he filed a petition seeking access to his more than $1.5 million trust fund to help pay for his defense. KABC reported that Jake Reiner isn’t commenting about his brother’s attempts to access money from the trust.

articles.title: Whistles, shouts warned Trishuli folks as river rose 30ft in 30 mins
articles.summary: South Asia News: Whistles and shouts became the last line of warning along stretches of Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river on Wednesday as the Nepal-Tibet flood tore downs.
articles.body: Whistles and shouts became the last line of warning along stretches of Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river on Wednesday as the Nepal-Tibet flood tore downstream, forcing residents to scramble up the banks while the river rose by nearly 30ft in just 30 minutes at one monitoring point.The speed of the rise left little margin for delay. ICIMOD said Trishuli at Galchhi rose by as much as nine metres — nearly 30ft — within 30 minutes, while Malekhu recorded a seven-metre rise over a similar period. Several monitoring stations were damaged or swept away as the flood moved downstream.Nepal’s warning system began sending alerts after authorities learnt of the flood, but the upper-basin network failed to provide advance notice. Binod Parajuli, senior divisional hydrologist at Flood Forecasting Division, said automatic stations in upper Bhote Koshi stopped transmitting before they could alert officials. “None of the stations was able to send us an alert,” he said.More than 600,000 SMS alerts were later sent to riverbank communities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan. Officials said those warnings helped many people farther downstream, but residents in some locations still had to rely on what they could see and hear around them. Parajuli acknowledged the uneven outcome. “We failed in Rasuwa,” he said. “But we sent warnings to Nuwakot and downstream areas, and possibly several hundred people were able to save their lives.”He said Nepal needed denser real-time monitoring and faster cross-border information sharing for sudden Himalayan hazards. “If we can install sensors extensively in the mountains and receive information as soon as an event occurs, we can give people downstream enough time to move to safety,” he said.--------------Box-------------------Chinese Embassy rejects claims it failed to issue timely warningChinese Embassy in Kathmandu on Thursday rejected allegations that China failed to provide timely warning about the devastating flood in Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border area, calling claims circulating in Nepal “fake news” and “misleading”. The embassy disputed two allegations — that Nepal suffered heavy casualties because China did not issue an early warning, and that a geological disaster dam on the Chinese side collapsed and caused widespread destruction downstream in Nepal.It said the sequence of events was different and maintained that a landslide triggered by an earthquake or an earthquake-like tremor occurred on the Nepali side on the morning of Aug 26, 2026. The clarification came amid questions in Nepal over whether timely upstream information could have reduced casualties.Chinese Embassy urged both countries to concentrate on search, rescue and relief operations instead of assigning blame. “Blame solves nothing; cooperation saves lives,” it said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Fiery views on Lindsay Clancy at work could get you fired — and be perfectly legal, employment lawyer warns
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has sparked heated workplace debates, but an employment law expert warns fiery opinions could legally get you fired.
articles.body: Sharing fiery views at work about the Massachusetts mom accused of killing her three young children could get you canned and still be legal, according to an expert on employment law who is following the case. Lindsay Clancy, 36, is accused of strangling her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office. The case has drawn national attention, pro-Clancy protesters to the courthouse and impassioned discussions about who is responsible online after her defense argued she is not guilty by reason of insanity or mental defect. articles.title: ‘Don’t need help’: Nepal declines foreign rescue teams as flood death toll nears 500
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal has declined offers from several countries to deploy search and rescue teams after devastating flash floods killed at least 469 people and left .
articles.body: Nepal has declined offers from several countries to deploy search and rescue teams after devastating flash floods killed at least 469 people and left hundreds missing, saying its own security agencies are capable of handling the operation.The decision comes as rescue teams continue to search through mud and debris following Wednesday’s flash flood along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems near the Nepal-China border.According to The Kathmandu Post, Nepal’s foreign ministry has received multiple official and unofficial requests from countries and international organisations seeking to send their own rescue personnel. Officials, however, said the government had decided that Nepali security agencies should lead the operation.India, China, the US, UK, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh were among those that sought to assist with search and rescue, the newspaper reported. India had also requested permission to deploy its National Disaster Response Force after hundreds of its citizens were reported missing. Nepal declined the request.“We received similar requests from China and other countries too, but we had to turn down the request,” a foreign ministry official told The Kathmandu Post."Don't need help with rescue operation from other countries," the ministry said, as per Reuters.The decision was partly based on Nepal’s experience after the 2015 earthquake, when the arrival of numerous foreign rescue teams created coordination and management difficulties, according to the report.Instead of foreign rescue teams, Nepal wants financial assistance channelled through a single mechanism. Officials said further international support would be sought during the rehabilitation and reconstruction phases.The scale of the disaster remains immense. Nepal Police said on Friday that 469 people had died, while 1,545 people had been rescued and injured. Nearly 1,000 people remain missing, according to disaster authorities, with 28 police personnel also unaccounted for.Nepal Police has deployed 4,348 personnel for search and rescue operations. Authorities have rescued 644 people from Rasuwa, 898 from Nuwakot and three from Dhading.Foreign nationals are among those missing. The Kathmandu Post reported that 178 Indians, 65 Americans, 51 Malaysians, 53 Ukrainians, 33 Britons, 35 Australians and 25 Canadians remain unaccounted for, alongside nationals from dozens of other countries. Chinese officials have also said at least 100 Chinese nationals are out of contact.Nepal has nevertheless welcomed international financial and humanitarian assistance. The United States has pledged $500,000, while the World Health Organization has sent emergency medical supplies.The foreign ministry has also established an Emergency Control Room to coordinate information, search and rescue efforts and consular assistance for foreign nationals affected by the floods.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Name dates back 400 years': Canada's Carney rejects Trump's 'Lake Ontario' name change to 'Lake America'
articles.summary: US News: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday (local time) rejected US President Donald Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, declari.
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday (local time) rejected US President Donald Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, declaring that the iconic water body would remain known as Lake Ontario “today and forever.”In a social media post following Trump’s signing of an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, Carney said the lake’s original name dates back 400 years, long before Canada and the United States existed in their current forms."The name of Lake Ontario derives from the Wendat word « Ontari’io », which means « the lake is beautiful, the lake is great. This name dates back more than 400 years, well before the Canadian Confederation and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America," the Canadian prime minister wrote on X."We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever," he added.Earlier, Trump signed the executive order directing the US geographic naming service to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” The decision applies to the lake’s official designation by US authorities, but Washington has no authority to compel Canada to adopt the new name.The move comes after Trump’s earlier decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” for use by the US government.He signed the Lake Ontario order at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, with a map of the Great Lakes — five lakes that straddle the border between the two countries — displayed behind him showing the words “Lake America” in large red letters over Lake Ontario.The “renaming” comes amid another escalation in the US-Canada trade dispute after talks broke down last week over what Canada described as “last-minute” changes by the US side, as well as disagreements over other key issues. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, while Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on goods worth a similar amount.Trump has repeatedly criticised Canada since returning to the White House last year. He has also suggested that Canada should become the "51st US state," despite the two neighbours being long-standing allies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Anthropic gets legal shield against Pentagon blacklisting in AI safety fight
articles.summary: US News: A US judge Thursday blocked the Pentagon from blacklisting Anthropic as a national security supply-chain risk, dealing a setback to the US military in.
articles.body: A US judge Thursday blocked the Pentagon from blacklisting Anthropic as a national security supply-chain risk, dealing a setback to the US military in its high-stakes dispute with the maker of Claude over restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence in warfare.US District Judge Rita Lin, a Biden appointee, ruled that the Pentagon’s decision to designate Anthropic as a supply-chain risk was "illegal and baseless", according to a 59-page order. She said the government could not use national security concerns as a justification for retaliating against companies over their policy positions."The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics," she wrote.The ruling follows a lawsuit filed by Anthropic in a California federal court challenging Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s decision to designate the AI company a national security supply-chain risk. The designation restricted Anthropic’s access to certain military contracts and marked the first public designation of a US company as a supply-chain risk under a government procurement law intended to protect military systems from foreign sabotage.Anthropic had resisted allowing the military to use its Claude AI models for US surveillance or autonomous weapons. The company has argued that current AI systems are not sufficiently reliable for safe use in autonomous weapons and has opposed domestic surveillance on rights grounds.Anthropic welcomed the court’s decision, saying it remained committed to working with the US government on national security applications of AI."focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The dispute escalated after Hegseth’s decision, which Anthropic said could cost it billions of dollars in lost business and cause reputational damage. The company argued that the Pentagon had exceeded its authority and retaliated against its position on AI safety.In its March 9 lawsuit, Anthropic alleged that the government had violated its First Amendment right to free speech by retaliating against its views on AI safety. It also argued that the Pentagon violated its Fifth Amendment right to due process by designating the company without giving it an opportunity to challenge the decision.Anthropic said the designation was unlawful, unsupported by facts and inconsistent with the military’s previous praise for Claude, its artificial intelligence model.The Justice Department disputed Anthropic’s claims, arguing that the company’s refusal to remove restrictions on the military use of its AI models could create uncertainty for the Pentagon over how Claude could be used. The government also warned that such uncertainty could risk disabling military systems during operations.The Justice Department said the Pentagon’s decision was based on Anthropic’s refusal to accept contractual terms rather than on the company’s views about AI safety.The legal dispute is not over. Anthropic has another lawsuit pending in Washington, D.C., challenging a separate Pentagon designation that could potentially prevent the company from securing civilian government contracts.The case highlights a growing conflict between the US government’s push to deploy advanced AI for national security and technology companies’ concerns about safeguards, autonomous weapons and surveillance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Serial rapist police officer passed vetting despite warnings
articles.summary: Alan Greer was investigated by police in 2002 and 2005 for making inappropriate phone calls to women, with one case resulting in a formal police caution.
articles.body:
A police officer - who was later exposed as a violent serial rapist - passed vetting checks to join the force despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record, BBC Disclosure can reveal.

Alan Greer was investigated by police in 2002 and 2005 for making inappropriate phone calls to women, with one case resulting in a formal police caution.

He was accepted into Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite vetting staff being aware of his previous offending.

The revelation comes a month after Police Scotland told the BBC there had been no "missed opportunities over the years" to identify Greer's offending sooner.

In response to further questions from the BBC, Police Scotland moved to clarify its earlier comments.

It said it had "provided answers to questions relating to Alan Greer's offending during the course of his police career" and did not believe it had been answering questions about his police vetting record.

Greer had been a police officer for 17 years when he took his own life in May, just days after a police raid on his home as part of an investigation into offences dating back to 2012.

Last month, the BBC revealed he had committed a series of attempted murders or serious sexual assaults, including raping a vulnerable woman just hours after meeting her on duty.

It has since emerged that Greer had contact with hundreds of sex workers throughout his police career, and violently assaulted many of them.

It is also understood he took inappropriate photographs of female colleagues while working in police officer safety training.

Police Scotland has so far identified 15 of Greer's victims, amid fears the true number is far greater.

When the BBC revealed the story last month, Assistant Chief Constable Lynn Ratcliff was asked if there had been any opportunities to stop Greer's offending earlier.

She said: "At this point, and we will keep it under review, there is nothing to suggest that there have been any missed opportunities over the years."

When pressed if there were no missed red flags, she said "At this stage, we've got no evidence to suggest that is the case…"

Asked if there were any vetting issues in relation to Greer, ACC Ratcliff said the vetting landscape is "markedly different" today, that Greer would not have passed current vetting checks, but she did not offer further details.

The assistant chief constable added that officers were now subject to annual integrity testing and routine re-vetting.

A BBC Disclosure investigation can now reveal:

Greer was investigated in 2002 by Strathclyde Police for making inappropriate phone calls to a woman in Glasgow. The case was reported to the procurator fiscal but no action was taken

The Metropolitan Police issued Greer with a formal police caution in 2005 after he was again caught making inappropriate phone calls, this time to a woman he knew in London

Four years later in 2009, Strathclyde Police accepted Greer into the force despite being aware of at least the formal police caution issued by the Metropolitan Police

Police Scotland has now confirmed that Strathclyde's vetting unit in 2009 was aware of Greer's 2005 police caution when he was applying for the job.

A partial paper vetting record exists for Greer and the caution is referenced.

The force said it was unclear whether the 2002 offence formed part of the interview process, or was known by vetting staff.

Sources say this 2002 "adverse trace" would "absolutely" have been discoverable on Greer's record.

A Strathclyde Police Standard Operating Procedures handbook for 2006 states: "The force should not recruit people with cautions or convictions, which may call into question the integrity of the applicant or the force."

A police source told the BBC: "Two reported crimes related to women before he joined should have been raising all sorts of alarm bells.

"He was clearly a menace from the off and should never have been allowed near a uniform to abuse his position."

Craig Naylor, chief inspector for HM Inspectorate of Constabulary in Scotland HMICS), led a review into Police Scotland vetting processes in 2023.

He said the vetting landscape in 2009, though not as strict as today, should still have meant Greer's past would preclude entry to the police.

He said: "My view is that he should never have got in at that point, and my view is that in the intervening period, I'm surprised that something didn't come up about that.

"When I've run vetting in the past, he would not have got in."

Asked by the BBC if these were missed opportunities to stop Greer joining the police, Naylor answered, "Yes".

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have been completely open and transparent around information which can be shared in relation to the ongoing investigation into Alan Greer.

"During an interview with the BBC on 20 July 2026 we provided answers to questions relating to Alan Greer's offending during the course of his policing career, which spanned almost 17 years.

"The investigation has not established any information during his career which could have resulted in his criminal behaviour being identified at an earlier stage.

"The recruitment and vetting process carried out by Strathclyde Police prior to Alan Greer joining in 2009 will form part of an independent and external review by the National Police Chiefs' Council.

"Our absolute priority throughout this investigation is to support victims. As work continues to identify and support everyone affected by this case it is imperative that we do not disclose any information which could be detrimental to that support."

A timeline of how Alan Greer's crimes came to light

The BBC has obtained a confidential briefing document about the case, "Operation Submarine", prepared by the investigation's SIO (senior investigating officer).

The document is dated 12 June this year, about four weeks before the BBC contacted Police Scotland over its intention to run a story about the case.

It is described as a "high level overview" into Greer's "significant serious sexual offending".

Point 3 of the document is headlined "Identified Criminality" and details of the 2002 and 2005 investigations are listed.

It states: "Within the current vetting regime, he would not have been granted Recruitment Vetting."

The document was provided to the Scottish government and the Scottish Police Authority (SPA), the oversight body tasked with holding senior officers to account.

Yet during a public board meeting of the SPA on 30 July, a week after the BBC broke the initial story, none of the SPA board put the details of Greer's vetting issue to DCC Alan Spiers, who was there in place of Chief Constable Jo Farrell.

Board member Chris Creegan asked DCC Spiers which of Strathclyde's previous vetting arrangements were of "particular relevance to this case and Alan Greer's own history" but did not press for an answer and no details of Greer's vetting record were disclosed.

The SPA told the BBC that only the authority's chairman Alistair Hay and chief executive Chris Brown, who were both present at the meeting, received the briefing about Greer's vetting - and that it had not been shared with Creegan.

It said operational briefings were not "routinely shared" with board members.

A spokesperson for the SPA said: "Three authority members raised a number of initial questions to seek assurance about the approach being taken, the impact on public confidence - and the assertion that significant changes to vetting regulations would mean an individual such as Alan Greer, would not be able to join policing today."

An HMICS inquiry in 2023 identified significant gaps in Police Scotland's vetting processes, including a failure to re-vet legacy staff since the forces merged in 2013.

Greer was one of about 8,800 police officers and staff who had still not been re-vetted, more than a third of the total workforce.

HMICS also reviewed certain vetting categories from a sample of about 10% of total applications (about 5,500 over four years) and found at least 29 cases where the risk posed by applicants had been "incorrectly assessed" by vetting officers.

HMICS made 15 recommendations, including an urgent review of all the identified problem cases as well as introducing annual integrity testing for officers and routine re-vetting every 10 years.

Eleven of the recommendations, including the review of the problem cases, have been fully discharged, with work ongoing on the rest.

HMICS chief inspector Craig Naylor said: "It is a concern...there are still people who are not vetted three years on [from the review]."

Following the review and in response to concern over high-profile vetting failures in England including the case of David Carrick , Police Scotland initiated a "historic data wash".

It was part of a vetting improvement plan "to identify any intelligence or allegations that needed further investigation".

The Anti-Corruption Unit (ACU) led the project, along with the force's vetting unit, and concluded: "No significant matters were uncovered that the force were not already aware of."

Police Scotland confirmed the data wash flagged nothing in relation to Greer.

Naylor told the BBC this was another missed opportunity to spot him sooner.

A police source told the BBC: "So the data wash was useless then? How can they say there were no missed opportunities to spot Greer sooner?

"The question is, how many more Alan Greers have they missed?"

Police Scotland added: "We have already stated publicly that the vetting landscape in 2026 is markedly different from that in 2009 and, under current arrangements, Alan Greer's application would not have progressed."

Production/additional reporting: Kevin Anderson and Carla Basu

articles.title: Sunderland Museum and Winter Gardens' last day before refurb
articles.summary: Sunderland's Museum and Winter Gardens will close for two years ahead of a near-£14m renovation.
articles.body:
A museum is preparing for its last visitors before closing for a £13.6m refurbishment scheduled to take two years.

The Sunderland Museum and Winter Gardens, which opened at its current location off Burdon Road in 1879, will shut on Saturday afternoon for repairs, the relocation of the main entrance, changes to the layout and the addition of two new galleries.

However Sea Change, the operator of the museum's cafe that is staffed by people with autism and learning disabilities, will permanently close.

Trina Murphy, manager of museum redevelopment at Sunderland City Council, said many visitors were coming to say goodbye to its most famous attraction, the 164-year-old Wallace the lion.

Responding to the cafe closure, Murphy said it had only been a short-term arrangement.

The building has gone through several changes over the years, with a major extension being added in the 1960s and again in 2001 when the Winter Gardens was opened.

Looking to the future, Murphy said: "I can't wait for that day when we cut that ribbon because it will be for the people of the city and for the staff.

"They deserve to see their museum developed."

She said some smaller exhibits will go on tour in the community during the closure, with "loan boxes" handed out to places including schools in order to keep them visible.

articles.title: 'Need overhaul of education system': Dipke on IIT Delhi suicide protest
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party founder Dipke has called for a “complete overhaul” of the country's education system following the death of 31-year-.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party founder Dipke has called for a “complete overhaul” of the country's education system following the death of 31-year-old IIT Delhi MSc Physics student Rishikesh Kumar. Dipke said that students need an environment where they feel “supported, heard and hopeful about their future”.In a post on X, Dipke wrote: “IITs, considered among the best educational institutions in our country, have witnessed 65 student suicides in the last five years. If this is the situation at our best institutions, imagine the state of the rest. We need a complete overhaul of our education system, one that creates an environment where students feel supported, heard and hopeful about their future, rather than leaving them isolated, overwhelmed and struggling in silence.”Rishikesh died on August 22 after falling from the sixth floor of the Lecture Hall Complex. Police have said no suicide note was recovered and the circumstances surrounding his death are being investigated.Dipke's remarks came as IIT Delhi moved to constitute a final external inquiry committee to investigate the circumstances surrounding Rishikesh's death.The committee will be headed by retired Delhi high court judge Justice Mukta Gupta and will include Professor Pratap Sharan, head of the Department of Psychiatry at AIIMS New Delhi, four student representatives and IIT Delhi Registrar, who will serve as secretary and convenor, sources told ANI.The panel will interact with students, faculty members and administrative officials, review existing protocols and processes, and recommend measures to strengthen student support systems. It has been asked to submit its report within two weeks.The committee was reconstituted after former Uttarakhand DGP Ashok Kumar, who had initially been proposed as chairperson, recused himself citing prior commitments. Students had earlier demanded that the inquiry be headed by a former High Court judge.The earlier committee was announced by IIT Delhi Director Professor Rangan Banerjee after protests over Rishikesh's death. Students had demanded an independent probe, the resignation of the Dean of Student Welfare and financial assistance for his family.Rishikesh joined IIT Delhi in July 2025 and was staying in a campus hostel. The institute said he had received counselling and medical treatment after concerns were raised by fellow students following Holi celebrations. His requests to withdraw from the second and third semesters were also approved.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'High risk' of lake bursting and causing second flood, warns China
articles.summary: China says a lake formed after a recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may burst in the coming days.
articles.body:
China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may burst, causing a second flood downstream.

The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river .

As of Friday morning, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated at the barrier lake, according to state broadcaster CCTV. A barrier lake is a body of water formed when debris dams up a river.

Officials said that three million cubic metres of water is expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and Saturday, posing a "high risk of breach".

The barrier lake, which formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, has already started to overflow, according to China's Ministry of Water Resources. The area has also seen heavy rain.

Authorities have sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions.

A CCTV report on Friday morning said that most of the Chinese emergency services were stuck at a village about 7km (4 miles) from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood.

This was because the barrier lake was "overflowing non-stop" which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows.

Due to the risks, search and rescue operations had to be suspended near the Nepal-Tibet border, according to the report.

The lake is in the same region as the Langtang Lirung peak, where the collapsed glacier is believed to have originated, and several kilometres upstream from Gyirong Port.

Separately, Nepali authorities have warned of the risk of blockages causing further floods along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers.

They have warned people to stay away from the rivers until further notice.

Scientists have said that the flood on Wednesday was likely to have been caused by part of a glacier near Langtang Lirung collapsing into the river below, which in turn caused a massive surge downstream carrying water and debris.

Several hundred people have died in Nepal and with hundreds more still missing after the flash flood. On the Tibet side of the border alone, more than 550 are missing - nearly half of which are foreigners.
